title: Safe administration and medicines errors
blurb: Carry out the checks before every dose, avoid medication Never Events, respond openly to an error and report suspected adverse reactions through the Yellow Card scheme.
question: On a busy postnatal ward, midwife Kate realises she has just given IV cyclizine to Mrs Ali in bay 2 instead of Mrs Ali in bay 4. What should she do, and in what order?

teach.h: Safe administration is a set of checks, every time
teach.body: The NMC withdrew its old medicines standards; the RPS/RCN Professional guidance on the administration of medicines (2019) now applies UK-wide, alongside Code standard 18 (use medicines within your training, the law and guidance). Formally, a medication error is any preventable event in prescribing, dispensing, preparing, administering or monitoring a medicine that may cause harm. In plain English: most medicine harm comes from a skipped check, and most errors are caught by a midwife who stops and checks again.

head: Check
Why
rows: Identity of the woman or baby
Name, form or route, strength, dose
By a second person where practicable
teach.caption: Record every medicine given, withheld or declined at the time or as soon as possible, with the reason, and tell the prescriber where needed.

items: Verbal orders: exceptional circumstances only, and never for a Schedule 2 controlled drug; the prescriber confirms in writing, ideally within 24 hours.
Transcribing: only within an organisational policy, by trained staff, with an audit trail; never transcribe illegible or ambiguous details.
Ambiguous prescription (for example 'u' for units): do not guess; ask the prescriber to rewrite it.
Code 18.3: check that the medicine is compatible with others the woman takes, including over-the-counter medicines.

steps.label: Act immediately
steps.sub: assess and protect the woman or baby (Code 14.1)

steps.label: Record and learn
steps.sub: facts in the notes; PSIRF learning

teach.caption: If the incident caused moderate harm or worse, the statutory duty of candour applies: notify her in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with a true account and an apology, then in writing (reg 20). An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006 s2).

teach.h: Never Events relevant to midwives (2018 list, updated 2021)
head: Never Event
Barrier
rows: Oral or enteral medicine given by a parenteral route
Insulin overdose from abbreviations or wrong device
'Units' in full; insulin syringe or pen
Retained foreign object after a procedure
Swab counts, incl. after vaginal birth and perineal repair
teach.caption: Never Events are 'wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations that provide strong systemic protective barriers are available at a national level'.

teach.h: Yellow Card report or incident report?
teach.caption: Suspicion is enough for a Yellow Card: proof of cause is not needed. Children are a priority group.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Kate and the cyclizine
teach.body: Kate first goes to the woman in bay 2: she assesses her, takes observations and asks the doctor to review her, because putting things right comes first (Code 14.1). She also checks that the woman in bay 4 still receives the care she needs. She informs the midwife in charge, explains to the woman in bay 2 what happened and apologises, completes an incident report and records the facts in the notes. Two identical surnames on one ward is a system risk to raise, too.

teach.text: Do not mix up the two reports. A Yellow Card is for a suspected adverse REACTION to a medicine, even when it was given correctly. A wrong patient, dose, route or time is a medication ERROR, reported through the local incident system. Some events need both.

items: Check identity, prescription, consent, allergies, calculation and that the dose is not already given.
Verbal orders: exceptional, never for Schedule 2 CDs; never transcribe ambiguous details.
After an error: act to put it right, escalate, be open and apologise, report, record.
Never Events: oral medicines given IV, insulin abbreviation overdose, strong potassium, retained swabs.
Yellow Card: all suspected reactions to black-triangle medicines, serious ones for established medicines; anyone can report.

summary: You can now carry out the checks that make each administration safe, recognise the medication Never Events, and respond to an error by putting it right, being open and reporting. You can also tell when a Yellow Card report is needed.

A.q: Before giving a regular dose, which check specifically prevents a duplicate dose?
options: Checking the expiry date on the box
Checking it has not been given
Checking the allergy status
Checking the storage needs
A.why: RPS/RCN guidance includes checking that the dose has not already been given, which prevents duplicate administration.

whyNot.0: Expiry checks protect against an outdated medicine, not a repeat dose.
whyNot.2: Allergy checks prevent a known harm, not a second dose.
whyNot.3: Storage checks protect the medicine's quality, not the timing of doses.

A.q: An obstetrician phones the labour ward and asks the midwife to give oxycodone, a Schedule 2 controlled drug, saying she will write it up later. What should the midwife do?
options: Give it and get it written within 24 hours
Give it if a second midwife also hears the call
Transcribe it onto the chart and give it
Decline and ask for a written prescription
A.why: RPS/RCN: verbal orders are for exceptional circumstances only and are never used for a Schedule 2 controlled drug.

whyNot.0: Confirmation within 24 hours applies to permitted verbal orders, not Schedule 2 CDs.
whyNot.1: A witness to the call does not make a verbal Schedule 2 order acceptable.
whyNot.2: Transcribing copies an existing prescription; writing up a phoned Schedule 2 order is not transcribing (RPS/RCN 24).

A.q: A woman develops symptoms after a black-triangle medicine. Which reactions to that medicine should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme?
options: Serious reactions, once cause is proven
Reactions confirmed by a doctor
Any suspected reaction, serious or not
Reactions within the first week of use
A.why: MHRA: report all suspected reactions to black-triangle medicines (and serious ones for established medicines); suspicion is enough.

whyNot.0: Proof of cause is not needed, and black-triangle medicines need all reactions reported.
whyNot.1: Anyone, including the woman, can report; a doctor's confirmation is not required.
whyNot.3: There is no time window: suspected reactions are reported whenever they occur.

B.q: Midwife Kate realises she has given IV cyclizine to the wrong woman. What should she do first?
options: Assess the woman, do observations and escalate
Complete the incident report before anything else
Tell the midwife in charge at the end of the shift
Record it and review her at the next drug round
B.why: Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation. The woman's safety comes first, then escalation, openness, reporting and documentation.

whyNot.1: Reporting matters, but the woman's safety comes first.
whyNot.2: Delaying escalation to the end of the shift risks harm.
whyNot.3: Waiting for the next round delays assessment of possible harm.

B.q: A medication error caused Sara moderate harm. Under the statutory duty of candour, what must happen?
options: A letter of apology is sent within 3 months
In person with an apology, then in writing
She is told if the harm becomes permanent
The consultant decides whether to tell her
B.why: Regulation 20: notify the person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, with a true account and an apology, followed by written notification.

whyNot.0: Notification is in person and as soon as reasonably practicable, not a delayed letter.
whyNot.2: Moderate harm already triggers the duty; permanence is not required.
whyNot.3: Candour is a duty, not a discretionary decision.

B.q: Which of these incidents is a Never Event?
options: A PPH of 1,200 mL after vaginal birth
A third-degree tear at a forceps birth
A swab left in the vagina after a repair
A 2-hour delay in giving labour pain relief
B.why: Retained foreign object after a procedure is a Never Event; the definition includes interventions related to vaginal birth, such as swabs after perineal suturing.

whyNot.0: A PPH is a serious complication, but not on the Never Events list.
whyNot.1: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is a recognised complication, not a Never Event.
whyNot.3: Delayed pain relief is a staffing red flag (NICE NG4), not a Never Event.

C.q: Grace has type 1 diabetes and is in labour. Her insulin is prescribed as '6u' per hour. What should the midwife do?
options: Give 6 units an hour, as the meaning is clear
Ask the prescriber to write 'units' in full
Amend it to '6 units' herself and start it
Start it and ask for a correction at handover
C.why: 'Units' must be written in full; 'u' can be misread (for example as a zero), and insulin overdose from abbreviations is a Never Event. Never act on, or transcribe, an ambiguous prescription.

whyNot.0: An abbreviated insulin prescription is ambiguous and must be corrected first.
whyNot.2: Midwives must not alter or transcribe ambiguous prescription details.
whyNot.3: Starting before correction leaves the hazard in place.

C.q: A midwife is preparing an oral liquid medicine for a baby. Which practice prevents a medication Never Event?
options: Use any 5 mL syringe that is to hand
Measure it with a standard IV (Luer) syringe
Draw up all doses before the round starts
Measure it in an oral or enteral syringe
C.why: Giving an oral or enteral medicine by a parenteral route is a Never Event; the national barrier is measuring oral liquids in oral/enteral syringes that cannot connect to IV devices.

whyNot.0: A random syringe may be an IV syringe that fits an IV line.
whyNot.1: IV syringes allow oral medicines to be given by the wrong route.

C.q: Mariam, on the postnatal ward, develops a widespread rash after her first correctly given dose of a new black-triangle antibiotic. Beyond treating her and recording the allergy, what reporting is appropriate?
options: A Yellow Card report of the suspected reaction
An incident report logged as a medication error
No report until allergy tests confirm it
A referral of the midwife to the NMC
C.why: A suspected adverse reaction to a black-triangle medicine should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme; suspicion is enough.

whyNot.1: The dose was given correctly, so this is an adverse reaction, not an error.
whyNot.2: Yellow Card reports do not need proof of cause.
whyNot.3: There is no professional failing to refer.

reteach.title: Stop, check, own it
reteach.question: What separates a near miss from a harmful error, and what does a good midwife do when something goes wrong?

blocks.body: Most errors happen when a check is skipped under pressure: two women with the same name, an abbreviated prescription, an IV syringe used for an oral medicine. The pause to confirm identity, prescription, dose, route and timing is the safety barrier. When an error does happen, the Code expects you to act at once to put it right, be honest with the woman and help the system learn.

blocks.text: Saying sorry is not admitting negligence (Compensation Act 2006 s2). Being open is a professional duty (Code 14).

explain.body: RPS/RCN guidance lists the checks before administration, including that calculations are double-checked by a second person where practicable.

test.q: A dose needs a calculation. What does RPS/RCN guidance advise?
options: Round it to the nearest whole ampoule
The woman checks the sum herself
A second person double-checks it
A pharmacist attends before every dose
test.why: RPS/RCN: calculations are double-checked by a second person where practicable.

whyNot.0: Rounding to an ampoule changes the prescribed dose.
whyNot.1: Involving the woman is good practice, but the professional check is a second person.
whyNot.3: Pharmacist attendance is not required for every calculated dose.

explain.body: Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation if someone has suffered actual harm for any reason or an incident has happened which had the potential for harm. Then explain, apologise and document.

items.label: act immediately to put it right

test.q: After a medication mistake, what does NMC Code 14.1 require first?
options: Inform the NMC within 24 hours
Act immediately to put the situation right
Wait for the outcome of a formal investigation
Ask a colleague to tell the woman
test.why: Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation.

whyNot.0: Self-referral to the NMC is not the first step after an error.
whyNot.2: Waiting delays action that may prevent harm.
whyNot.3: The professional involved should be open with the woman.

explain.body: Never Events are 'wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations that provide strong systemic protective barriers are available at a national level and should have been implemented by all healthcare providers' (NHS England).

test.q: What makes an incident a Never Event?
options: It caused the death of a woman or a baby
It recurred three times on the unit in a year
It involved a controlled drug
Strong national barriers make it preventable
test.why: Never Events are defined by being wholly preventable because strong systemic protective barriers exist nationally and should have been implemented.

whyNot.0: A Never Event need not cause death; it is defined by preventability.
whyNot.1: Frequency does not define a Never Event.
whyNot.2: CD involvement does not by itself make an event a Never Event.

explain.body: The MHRA Yellow Card scheme collects suspected adverse drug reactions and device problems. Anyone can report, including the woman herself; suspicion is enough.

test.q: A woman asks if she can report a suspected side effect herself through the Yellow Card scheme. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, anyone can report a suspected reaction
No, a doctor must submit the report
No, her midwife must report it for her
Yes, but once a doctor has confirmed the cause
test.why: MHRA: anyone, including patients, can submit a Yellow Card report, and suspicion is enough.

whyNot.1: Doctors can report, but so can anyone else.
whyNot.2: Professionals may report, but she can also report directly.
whyNot.3: Proof or confirmation of cause is not needed.
